My Price is My Life | Setting Sail with Whistleblower Jodi O’Malley and James O’Keefe Episode #4

Whistleblower Jodi O’Malley comes aboard the Lucky Charm III to share what her life’s been like since she heroically exposed how the federal government was handling (and allegedly hiding) adverse reactions to the COVID-19 vaccine.

In 2021, Jodi was a nurse at the Phoenix Indian Medical Center, a facility under the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). She tells James how the Holy Spirit prompted her to hit “record” while her concerned colleagues, including physicians, were discussing patients they believed were suffering adverse effects from the vaccine, reactions that weren't being formally reported. Thus, igniting Jodi’s ongoing advocacy in nursing.

Jodi also shares other challenging moments in her life that strengthened her faith and trust in God, leading her to the work and mission she’s tackling now.

Julian Assange has given a stark account of what he says unfolded after WikiLeaks published material that powerful institutions wanted buried. He says the CIA drew up plans to kidnap and assassinate him inside the Ecuadorian Embassy in London, authorized action against his European colleagues, and subjected those around him to theft, hacking, and the planting of false information.

Assange says the campaign did not stop with him. A CIA asset was permanently assigned to track his wife. Instructions were given to obtain DNA from his six-month-old son’s nappy. A baby’s diaper. A child’s genetic material. That is the allegation he places on the record: an intelligence operation that reached into his family after WikiLeaks exposed files tied to Hillary Clinton, John Podesta, Barack Obama, and other figures who wanted the leaks contained.

The Clinton remark now resurfacing is the line attributed to her while officials hunted ways to cut off the cables and limit the damage: “Can’t we just drone this guy?” In that telling, WikiLeaks was not treated as journalism. Assange was treated as a problem to be removed.

The larger question attached to his account is familiar to anyone who watched the war on Donald Trump. If agencies and political operators would plan a kidnapping, hunt a wife, seek an infant’s DNA, and float a drone strike to stop exposure, why assume they would stop short of a fabricated Russia narrative, the silencing of Seth Rich, lawfare, bankruptcy schemes, or election interference when their grip on power was at risk?

Assange turns the story away from personalities. He says he was convicted by a foreign power for asking for, receiving, and publishing truthful information while he was in Europe. “The criminalization of news gathering activities is a threat to investigative journalism everywhere,” he warns. “Journalists should not be prosecuted for doing their jobs. Journalism is not a crime; it is a pillar of a free and informed society.”

That is the core. If publishing the truth can bring alleged assassination plans and a hunt for a baby’s DNA, the target was never only Julian Assange. It was whether anyone is still allowed to expose the powerful without becoming the next name on the list. Journalism is not a crime.
